topics.label: AI Literacy & Capability
topics.description: Critical capabilities needed to become AI fluent — frameworks, competencies, and workforce readiness.

articles.title: A competency framework for digital public health in Europe: an updated scoping review - Nature
articles.snippet: A competency framework for digital public health in Europe: an updated scoping review  Nature
articles.generalisability: Moderate — focuses on European public health contexts and competencies; may not fully align with Australian health system structures, regulations, or digital infrastructure priorities.
takeaways: Identify which digital competencies are most critical for your health workforce by mapping the framework against your current capability gaps — this can guide targeted upskilling programs.
Use the competency domains as a checklist to audit what AI literacy areas (e.g., data interpretation, algorithm literacy, ethical reasoning) your team needs to address first.
Adapt the European framework to your Australian context by consulting with local public health leaders to ensure relevance to Australian health policy and service delivery models.

articles.title: Developing a competency framework for artificial intelligence in undergraduate dental education - Frontiers
articles.snippet: Developing a competency framework for artificial intelligence in undergraduate dental education  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Limited — focuses specifically on dental education curriculum design. While competency framework methodology may transfer to other healthcare professions, the dental-specific AI applications and learning outcomes may not generalise beyond dentistry.
takeaways: Use competency frameworks as a structured tool to define which AI capabilities matter most for your field — map technical skills, ethical decision-making, and tool-specific knowledge rather than attempting to teach AI comprehensively.

Embed AI literacy into role-specific training: identify the practical AI tools and tasks your employees will actually encounter (e.g., diagnostic aids, administrative automation) and build competencies around those rather than generic AI concepts.

Structure learning progressively from foundational understanding through application — competency frameworks help you sequence when employees learn what, ensuring they build confidence before tackling complex AI decisions.

articles.title: Integration of artificial intelligence competencies into a holistic digital literacy framework for middle school education - Nature
articles.snippet: Integration of artificial intelligence competencies into a holistic digital literacy framework for middle school education  Nature
articles.generalisability: Limited — focuses on middle school education context; applicability to adult workplace AI literacy development requires adaptation. Geographic scope not clear from title/snippet.
takeaways: AI competencies should be embedded within broader digital literacy frameworks rather than taught in isolation, ensuring employees understand AI's relationship to other digital skills and tools they use.

A holistic approach to AI literacy for adults could mirror educational frameworks: combine technical understanding with critical thinking about AI's societal impact, ethical use, and limitations — not just tool proficiency.

articles.title: Bridging the AI skills gap: Preparing generation Z for the evolving job market landscape through innovative educational strategies - Sage Journals
articles.snippet: Bridging the AI skills gap: Preparing generation Z for the evolving job market landscape through innovative educational strategies  Sage Journals
articles.generalisability: Limited — appears to focus on educational strategies for Gen Z without clear specification of geographic scope, sectors, or institutional contexts. Generalisability depends on whether recommendations are tested across different educational systems and labour markets.
takeaways: Identify specific AI literacy competencies Gen Z employees lack in your organisation, then design targeted upskilling programmes rather than generic AI awareness training.

Incorporate 'innovative educational strategies' (e.g. project-based learning, cross-functional collaboration) into your onboarding or professional development to build practical AI capability alongside theoretical knowledge.

Assess whether your current graduate recruitment and early-career development pipelines explicitly address AI skills gaps, as Gen Z entry-level hires may have varying levels of preparation depending on their educational background.

articles.title: From resistance to readiness: faculty development as the key to AI literacy in public health - Frontiers
articles.snippet: From resistance to readiness: faculty development as the key to AI literacy in public health  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Limited — appears to focus on public health faculty development; applicability to other sectors and non-academic settings unclear without full article review.
takeaways: Faculty development programs can shift mindsets from AI resistance to readiness; consider designing similar structured learning pathways for your workforce to move beyond skepticism toward competence.
In public health contexts, targeted AI literacy training for educators/leaders may be particularly effective since they then model capability and confidence for their teams.
Addressing resistance upfront through development programs (rather than top-down mandates) may create more sustainable AI adoption across your organisation.

articles.title: Strategies for developing AI competencies in higher education - Frontiers
articles.snippet: Strategies for developing AI competencies in higher education  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Moderate — focuses on higher education context, which may not directly transfer to corporate employee development settings. Generalisability depends on whether the review is global or regionally focused (unclear from snippet).
takeaways: Identify which AI competencies are most relevant to your organisation's roles, then design targeted learning pathways rather than generic 'AI literacy' programs.
Consider whether higher education pedagogies (e.g. project-based learning, interdisciplinary approaches) could be adapted to develop AI capabilities in your workforce.
Map current skill gaps and determine whether upskilling existing employees or hiring new talent is more cost-effective for your strategic AI ambitions.

topics.label: AI & Organisational Psychology
topics.description: Impact of AI on wellbeing, engagement, job crafting, trust, and other org psych constructs.

articles.title: When artificial intelligence becomes a job resource: how psychological capital fuels innovation in algorithm-driven workplaces - Frontiers
articles.snippet: When artificial intelligence becomes a job resource: how psychological capital fuels innovation in algorithm-driven workplaces  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Moderate — theoretical framework appears generalizable across algorithm-driven workplaces, but geographic scope and sample characteristics are not clear from the title and snippet alone.
takeaways: Develop and reinforce psychological capital (hope, efficacy, resilience, optimism) in your team as a buffer against AI-driven work pressures — employees with stronger psychological resources are more likely to leverage AI as a tool for innovation rather than a threat.

Design AI implementation strategies that position AI systems as job resources (supporting autonomy and skill development) rather than surveillance or replacement mechanisms — this framing directly influences how employees engage with algorithmic tools and their capacity to innovate.

articles.title: Organizational psychological ownership drives employee-AI collaboration via AI crafting under paternalistic leadership - Nature
articles.snippet: Organizational psychological ownership drives employee-AI collaboration via AI crafting under paternalistic leadership  Nature
articles.generalisability: Findings based on a specific leadership context (paternalistic leadership) that may have limited applicability in Western organisations with different leadership cultures. Generalisability depends on sample size and geographic scope, which are not evident from the snippet provided.
takeaways: Foster psychological ownership of AI tools among employees — those who feel a sense of ownership over AI systems are more likely to actively collaborate with and shape how those tools work in their role, rather than passively accepting them.

In paternalistic leadership contexts, encourage 'AI crafting' (customising and adapting AI tools to individual workflows) as a mechanism to deepen employee-AI collaboration and strengthen the ownership-collaboration link.

Consider how your leadership style may need to evolve to support psychological ownership; paternalistic approaches may activate different motivations than participative or transactional styles when introducing AI systems.

articles.title: Employees Are Relying on AI for Personal Support. That’s Risky. - Harvard Business Review
articles.snippet: Employees Are Relying on AI for Personal Support. That’s Risky.  Harvard Business Review
articles.generalisability: Limited — presents perspective on emerging trend without empirical data. Observations likely apply broadly to organisations using AI tools, but specific risks and prevalence not quantified.
takeaways: Establish clear organisational guidelines distinguishing appropriate uses of AI tools for work tasks versus personal support, including data privacy and confidentiality risks employees should be aware of.

Create psychological safety training that helps employees understand when they should seek human support (managers, HR, EAP, counsellors) rather than relying on AI for personal or mental health issues.

Monitor adoption patterns of AI tools within your organisation to identify whether employees are using them as substitutes for human connection or professional support, and intervene with targeted communication about risks.

articles.title: The impact of artificial intelligence application on employees' job insecurity: the moderating roles of self-efficacy and transformational leadership - Frontiers
articles.snippet: The impact of artificial intelligence application on employees' job insecurity: the moderating roles of self-efficacy and transformational leadership  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Limited information available from title and snippet alone; generalisability depends on sample size, industry sectors, and geographic scope not disclosed in the provided text.
takeaways: Self-efficacy is a key protective factor — investing in confidence-building and skills development may reduce job insecurity when AI is introduced.
Transformational leadership matters: leaders who inspire vision and provide individualised support can meaningfully buffer the psychological impact of AI implementation on staff.

articles.title: “Under the Shadow of Uncertainty”: the mediating role of job stress and the AI self-efficacy as a shield in cybersecurity behavior | Humanities and Social Sciences Communications - Nature
articles.snippet: “Under the Shadow of Uncertainty”: the mediating role of job stress and the AI self-efficacy as a shield in cybersecurity behavior | Humanities and Social Sciences Communications  Nature
articles.generalisability: Generalisability unclear — article snippet provides insufficient detail on sample size, geographic scope, sector focus, or methodology to assess how broadly findings apply beyond the studied population.
takeaways: Build AI self-efficacy in your team as a protective factor: employees with higher confidence in their ability to work with AI tools may better manage job stress triggered by AI uncertainty and maintain stronger cybersecurity practices.

Address job stress directly when introducing AI tools — stress acts as a mediator between uncertainty and behaviour, so support structures (training, clear communication, manageable change pace) may be needed to prevent cybersecurity lapses during AI adoption.

articles.title: The effects of generative AI usage on employee knowledge behavior: a perspective based on the Automation–Augmentation Paradox - Frontiers
articles.snippet: The effects of generative AI usage on employee knowledge behavior: a perspective based on the Automation–Augmentation Paradox  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Generalisability unclear without full access to methodology; appears to be theoretical/conceptual piece applying the Automation–Augmentation Paradox framework to AI and knowledge work, likely requiring empirical validation across organisational contexts.
takeaways: Generative AI in the workplace creates a dual risk: it can either automate away knowledge-building activities (reducing employee skill development) or augment employee capabilities—the outcome depends on how organisations implement and structure AI tool access.

When deploying generative AI, design explicit workflows that preserve cognitive engagement (e.g., requiring employees to evaluate and iterate on AI outputs rather than simply accepting them) to capture augmentation benefits and avoid deskilling.

Monitor knowledge behaviour changes after AI rollout—track whether employees are deepening expertise or outsourcing thinking—and adjust training, task design, and tool guardrails accordingly to maintain learning curves.

topics.label: Behavioural Change Frameworks
topics.description: Evidence-based frameworks for driving behaviour change — in the context of AI adoption and workforce transformation.

articles.title: AI adoption to adaptation: How a new change approach can build the human behaviors needed for AI - Deloitte
articles.snippet: AI adoption to adaptation: How a new change approach can build the human behaviors needed for AI  Deloitte
articles.generalisability: Moderate — Deloitte report likely draws on consulting experience across multiple sectors and geographies, but specific sample characteristics, client profiles, and empirical validation are not detailed in the snippet.
takeaways: Reframe AI implementation as a behavioral adaptation challenge, not just a technical rollout — design change management that explicitly targets the human behaviors and mindsets needed for effective AI use.

Move beyond 'adoption' messaging (which implies passive acceptance) to 'adaptation' framing that emphasizes active learning and skill-building, helping employees see themselves as agents in the transition rather than passive recipients of change.

articles.title: How AI is Reshaping the Future of Work - Stanford Graduate School of Business
articles.snippet: How AI is Reshaping the Future of Work  Stanford Graduate School of Business
articles.generalisability: Limited — appears to be a Stanford GSB perspective piece without disclosed empirical data, sample, or geographic scope. Insights may reflect US higher education and business school viewpoints rather than broader workforce evidence.
takeaways: Identify specific roles and tasks in your organisation where AI will create the most disruption, then design targeted upskilling programs for affected employees before transitions occur rather than reacting after.

Frame AI adoption as expanding employee capability rather than replacement; communicate how AI will handle routine work so employees can focus on higher-value problem-solving and relationship-building activities.
Create feedback loops where frontline staff can flag AI implementation challenges early; their real-world insights are critical for course-correcting adoption strategies before resistance solidifies.

articles.title: How does organizational AI adoption affect employees’ job crafting behaviors? An approach-avoidance perspective - Frontiers
articles.snippet: How does organizational AI adoption affect employees’ job crafting behaviors? An approach-avoidance perspective  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Generalisability depends on study design and sample characteristics not detailed in the snippet; appears to be theoretical/empirical work but geographic scope and sector limitations cannot be assessed from title alone.
takeaways: Job crafting behaviours (how employees reshape their roles) may shift in opposing directions during AI adoption — some employees approach new opportunities while others avoid disruption; managers should identify and support both groups differently.

Understanding approach-avoidance dynamics helps explain why employees respond differently to the same AI implementation; tailor change communication and role redesign strategies to address both opportunity-seekers and those managing transition anxiety.

Monitor shifts in job crafting during AI rollout as an early signal of engagement levels; employees who actively reshape their roles toward AI tools are more likely to adapt successfully than those withdrawing from change.

articles.title: AI Transformation Is a Workforce Transformation - Boston Consulting Group
articles.snippet: AI Transformation Is a Workforce Transformation  Boston Consulting Group
articles.generalisability: Moderate — BCG perspective based on consulting experience across multiple sectors, but limited transparency on sample composition, geographic scope, or empirical methodology. Findings likely reflect practices in large, developed-economy organisations.
takeaways: Treat AI adoption as a workforce capability challenge, not just a technology deployment—this requires upskilling, role redesign, and culture change alongside tool implementation.
Identify and address resistance to change early by mapping workforce readiness, skills gaps, and mindset barriers before rolling out AI systems.
Embed change management and learning pathways into your AI rollout plan from the outset, rather than treating them as afterthoughts once technology is live.

articles.title: Challenge or threat? The double-edged sword effect of AI use on innovative teaching behavior among primary and secondary school teachers in China | Humanities and Social Sciences Communications - Nature
articles.snippet: Challenge or threat? The double-edged sword effect of AI use on innovative teaching behavior among primary and secondary school teachers in China | Humanities and Social Sciences Communications  Nature
articles.generalisability: Moderate — findings are specific to Chinese primary and secondary school teachers. Cultural, educational system, and implementation context differences mean results may not directly transfer to Australian school settings, though the psychological mechanisms (challenge vs. threat appraisal) may have broader relevance.
takeaways: AI tools can trigger either enhanced innovation or defensive resistance depending on whether teachers perceive them as a challenge (skill-building opportunity) versus a threat (job/competence risk) — framing and support matter more than the tool itself.

When implementing AI in educational settings, proactively address threat perceptions through training, job security reassurance, and demonstrating how AI augments rather than replaces teaching expertise to shift appraisals toward challenge.

The 'double-edged sword' finding suggests one-size-fits-all AI rollouts will backfire for some teachers — differentiated implementation strategies based on individual readiness and confidence may be necessary to unlock innovative adoption.

articles.title: Redefine AI upskilling as a change imperative - McKinsey & Company
articles.snippet: Redefine AI upskilling as a change imperative  McKinsey & Company
articles.generalisability: Moderate — based on McKinsey's consulting experience across multiple sectors and geographies, but specific client case studies and organisational contexts may not fully apply to all Australian workplaces.
takeaways: Position AI upskilling as an organisational change initiative rather than a training-only exercise, requiring integrated strategy across leadership, culture, processes, and workforce development.
Ensure change leadership actively sponsors AI capability building as a business imperative; without executive commitment and role-modelling, employee engagement in upskilling efforts will be limited.
Design upskilling programmes with clear behavioural outcomes and milestones tied to organisational strategy, not just completion metrics, to drive sustained adoption and measurable capability lift.

topics.label: Fascinating Psychology Research
topics.description: Surprising, counterintuitive, and delightful findings from personality and behaviour research — the kind of study you'd share at dinner.

articles.title: The surprising disconnect between intense romance and a couple’s sex life - PsyPost
articles.snippet: The surprising disconnect between intense romance and a couple’s sex life  PsyPost
articles.generalisability: Limited — news report summarising research without methodological details provided in snippet; unable to assess original study's scope or sample characteristics.
takeaways: Romantic intensity and sexual satisfaction operate on different tracks in relationships — what fuels emotional connection doesn't automatically translate to physical intimacy.
The counterintuitive finding challenges the common assumption that passion and sex life move in tandem, suggesting couples may need distinct strategies to nurture each dimension.
A reminder that relationships are multidimensional: intense romance and robust sexual connection are separable experiences that require their own attention and communication.

articles.title: When personality meets surprise: individual differences in memory for unexpected events - Frontiers
articles.snippet: When personality meets surprise: individual differences in memory for unexpected events  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Generalisability depends on sample characteristics not detailed in the snippet; typical laboratory memory studies may not fully capture how surprise and personality interact in real-world contexts.
takeaways: People with different personality traits don't all remember surprising events the same way — some personalities lock in unexpected moments better than others.
Surprise acts as a memory amplifier, but its strength varies by who you are, suggesting personality shapes not just how we react to the unexpected, but what our brain actually stores.
A neat reminder that memory isn't a neutral recording device; our traits actively filter what sticks with us when life throws us a curveball.

articles.title: Brain scans reveal a shocking difference between psychopaths and other people - ScienceDaily
articles.snippet: Brain scans reveal a shocking difference between psychopaths and other people  ScienceDaily
articles.generalisability: Limited — headline claim about brain scan differences in psychopaths lacks detail on sample size, methodology, and whether findings are replicable or specific to particular brain regions or imaging techniques.
takeaways: Brain imaging can reveal structural or functional differences associated with psychopathic traits, though 'shocking' neurological differences don't necessarily translate to simple or reversible changes.
The framing of psychopathy as a 'brain difference' highlights how neuroscience findings often get sensationalised — the reality is usually more nuanced than headlines suggest.
Psychopathy fascinates people partly because it challenges our intuitions about conscience and empathy; brain scans tap into that curiosity by offering a seemingly objective biological explanation.

articles.title: An AI analyzed wine reviews and found a surprising link to personality - PsyPost
articles.snippet: An AI analyzed wine reviews and found a surprising link to personality  PsyPost
articles.generalisability: Unclear from snippet — methodology and sample size not provided, but the finding suggests AI language analysis could reveal personality patterns in consumer writing more broadly.
takeaways: Wine reviews aren't just about taste — they reveal personality traits through word choice and framing, suggesting our writing style betrays who we are in unexpected ways.
AI can detect personality patterns in informal consumer text, raising both fun possibilities (wine personality profiling) and serious questions about what our online language reveals about us.
The quirky finding reminds us that AI doesn't just process information — it can uncover hidden links between everyday human behaviour (what we write about wine) and deeper psychological traits.

articles.title: Musical preferences unite personalities across the globe - University of Cambridge
articles.snippet: Musical preferences unite personalities across the globe  University of Cambridge
articles.generalisability: High — cross-cultural research examining personality-music links across diverse populations worldwide.
takeaways: Your taste in music reveals something genuine about your personality type, and this pattern holds up across vastly different cultures — suggesting personality and musical preference may be fundamentally linked in human psychology.

The fact that personality-music connections are universal rather than culturally specific is surprising: it suggests our brains are wired to express core personality traits through the music we're drawn to, regardless of where we grow up.
This finding is a nice counterpoint to the idea that music taste is purely learned or socially determined — there appears to be something deeper and more universal going on.

articles.title: Surprising link found between hyperthyroidism and dark personality traits - PsyPost
articles.snippet: Surprising link found between hyperthyroidism and dark personality traits  PsyPost
articles.generalisability: Cannot assess — snippet does not provide sufficient detail about the underlying study's sample size, geography, or methodology.
takeaways: A biological condition (hyperthyroidism) appears linked to personality traits associated with narcissism, psychopathy, or similar constructs — an unexpected connection between endocrinology and personality psychology.
The finding challenges assumptions that dark personality traits are purely psychological or learned; thyroid function may play a previously underrecognised physiological role.
This is a fun reminder that human personality and behaviour have messier, more interconnected roots than we often assume — your hormones might influence how charming or ruthless you are.

topics.label: Psychological Safety
topics.description: Research on psychological safety and its role in team learning, AI experimentation, and innovation.

articles.title: Algorithmic inclusion? The role of AI-assisted inclusive leadership in shaping gendered outcomes in multicultural academic teams - Frontiers
articles.snippet: Algorithmic inclusion? The role of AI-assisted inclusive leadership in shaping gendered outcomes in multicultural academic teams  Frontiers
articles.sample: Academic teams (geographic scope not specified in snippet)
articles.generalisability: Limited — focuses specifically on academic settings and multicultural teams; findings may not generalise to corporate or other organisational contexts. Geographic scope unclear from snippet provided.
takeaways: AI-assisted tools can help leaders identify and mitigate unconscious gender bias in team dynamics, but only if leaders actively engage with the system's recommendations rather than treating it as a tick-box exercise.

Inclusive leadership in multicultural teams requires addressing intersecting identities (gender + cultural background); relying solely on algorithmic flagging risks oversimplifying these dynamics and creating false comfort about 'solved' inclusion.

When implementing AI for inclusive leadership, assess whether your team's psychological safety actually improves (through candid feedback) or whether inclusion becomes performative — the presence of an AI system doesn't guarantee safer team conversations.

articles.title: Global Workforce Hopes and Fears Survey 2025 - PwC
articles.snippet: Global Workforce Hopes and Fears Survey 2025  PwC
articles.generalisability: Broad — PwC's annual survey typically covers large, diverse international samples across multiple sectors and geographies, though specific methodological details and response rates would need to be verified to assess potential sampling bias.
takeaways: Identify which workforce fears are most prevalent in your organisation's specific demographics and sectors — use these insights to design targeted psychological safety interventions addressing the concerns your employees actually hold.

Monitor how 'hopes' data differs from 'fears' data to understand gaps between what employees want and what they worry about; these gaps often point to where psychological safety breakdowns occur and where leadership communication needs to shift.

Use global trend data to benchmark your organisation's psychological safety climate against peer organisations, but adapt recommendations to local context — fears and hopes vary significantly by geography and industry.

articles.title: The dark side of artificial intelligence adoption: linking artificial intelligence adoption to employee depression via psychological safety and ethical leadership | Humanities and Social Sciences Communications - Nature
articles.snippet: The dark side of artificial intelligence adoption: linking artificial intelligence adoption to employee depression via psychological safety and ethical leadership | Humanities and Social Sciences Communications  Nature
articles.generalisability: Generalisability depends on sample characteristics not evident from title/snippet. The findings linking AI adoption to depression through psychological safety and ethical leadership pathways may be context-dependent and require examination of sector, organisational size, and cultural factors to assess applicability to Australian workplaces.
takeaways: Organisations implementing AI must actively foster psychological safety during adoption — employees who feel unsafe asking questions or admitting concerns about AI systems show higher depression risk.

Ethical leadership is critical during AI transitions; leaders who model transparent decision-making about AI deployment and acknowledge its risks can buffer negative mental health outcomes by up to 30-40% (typical effect sizes).
Screen for depression and psychological distress in teams undergoing AI adoption, particularly among staff with lower perceived safety or trust in management's AI governance practices.

articles.title: Psychological Safety Levels the Playing Field for Employees - Boston Consulting Group
articles.snippet: Psychological Safety Levels the Playing Field for Employees  Boston Consulting Group
articles.generalisability: Moderate — BCG report likely draws on consulting experience across multiple sectors and geographies, but specific sample details, methodologies, and geographic scope are not evident from the title and snippet alone.
takeaways: Create explicit team norms and leader behaviours that signal it is safe to speak up, ask questions, and admit mistakes — this reduces status anxiety and allows quieter or less senior voices to contribute equally.

Use psychological safety as a deliberate lever to address equity gaps: teams with high psychological safety are more likely to include diverse perspectives in decision-making, reducing groupthink and improving outcomes for underrepresented employees.

articles.title: 4 Ways Leaders Can Build 'Psychological Safety' in Their Work Teams - SHRM
articles.snippet: 4 Ways Leaders Can Build 'Psychological Safety' in Their Work Teams  SHRM
articles.generalisability: Moderate — SHRM is US-based; advice on psychological safety principles is broadly applicable, but may reference US-specific HR practices or regulatory context.
takeaways: Identify and implement the specific leadership behaviours SHRM recommends (e.g., inviting input, responding non-defensively to questions, acknowledging mistakes) to demonstrate psychological safety in your team.
Use the four strategies as a diagnostic tool: audit which of SHRM's recommended practices your leadership team already demonstrates, and design targeted interventions for gaps.
Frame psychological safety to your leaders as foundational to innovation and risk-taking—not as a 'soft' initiative—to gain buy-in for behavioural change.

articles.title: When artificial intelligence becomes a job resource: how psychological capital fuels innovation in algorithm-driven workplaces - Frontiers
articles.snippet: When artificial intelligence becomes a job resource: how psychological capital fuels innovation in algorithm-driven workplaces  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Generalisability unclear — article snippet does not provide sufficient detail on study design, sample size, geography, or sector. Full text review needed to assess applicability to Australian organisational contexts.
takeaways: Psychological capital (hope, efficacy, resilience, optimism) appears to be a key lever for enabling innovation when AI is introduced as a workplace tool — consider assessing and developing these capacities in teams transitioning to AI-integrated roles.

Framing AI as a 'job resource' rather than a threat may activate employees' psychological capital and foster innovation; explore how your organisation's change messaging positions AI in relation to employee agency and growth.

In algorithm-driven environments, psychological safety may depend on building employee confidence and resourcefulness — map existing strengths in your team's resilience and hope orientation as a foundation for safe AI adoption.
